newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SAirGroup dives into loss, but analyst cheer.
newsitem.headline: SAirGroup dives into loss, but analyst cheer.

text.p: SAirGroup , the newly-created holding company that includes the Swissair airline, on Friday reported a 497 million Swiss franc ($346 million) loss, but analysts shrugged off the loss and cheered the improved operating profit.
SAirGroup boosted its operating profit 40 percent to 344 million Swiss francs, but extraordinary charges of 567 million pushed it into a larger-than-expected net loss of 497 million.
"I am positively surprised and bullish," said Dieter Winet of Societe Generale Bank and Trust.
For the fourth year in a row, SAirGroup omitted a dividend payout to its shareholders.
Operating revenue for SAirGroup, which includes the world's second-largest catering firm Gate Gourmet and hotel chain Swissotels, rose to 8.2 billion francs from 7.0 billion.

To underscore its recent transformation from an airline group to a diversified corporate group, SAirGroup last year changed its name from the Swissair Group and set up a holding company with four separate operating divisions.
The net loss for SAirGroup was widely anticipated and its shares have performed strongly in recent months on expectation that it will strong strong profit gains in 1997.

The extraordinary charges comprise 300 million francs for future structural adjustment to Europe's liberalised skies and 267 million to fully write down the value of SAirGroup's 49.5 percent stake in Belgian partner Sabena SA.

Analysts said the full write-down of the Sabena stake was largely anticipated, but many were surprised by the 300 million franc restructuring charge and bemoaned the lack of details over over what the charge would cover.
"I am surprised by the 300 million charge, but the operating profit is positive," Susanne Borer of Bank Vontobel said.
SAirGroup declined to provide details of the charge, except to say it should improve its competitiveness.

"While resulting in a sizable loss for the year, these provisions should lay a sound foundation for further enhancing the SAirGroup's ability to compete in the newly-liberalised European air transport market," SAirGroup said in a statement.
In 1995 SAirGroup, then known as the Swissair Group, had a loss of 147 million francs after restructuring charges of 365 million, partially to cover the cost of cutting the workforce by 2,000 people.
Winet took the charge as a sign that SAirGroup was preparing for a new round of job cuts and salary reductions.
"I think SAirGroup is such a financially strong company that it's making a pre-emptive strike to be prepared for a worst-case scenario in Europe with further price cuts," said Winet.
Chris Tarry of Kleinwort Benson Securities also noted the improved operating performance and said the restrucuturing charges illustrated management's will to reach its goals.

"There is a tremendous determination to improve the performance of the company and the new management team is strongly positive and are prepared to act to achieve its goal of a 12 percent return on capital in 1998," Tarry said.
SAirGroup said the operating result of SAirLines division were "less than satisfactory" in 1996, but it gave no figures.

SAirLines includes the flight operations of the Swissair airline, regional airline Crossair AG, Balair/CTA and the cooperation activities with the group's partner airlines, such as Sabena SA and Austrian Airlines AUA.

SAirGroup acquired the stake in Sabena in 1995 with the aim of developing a leading European airline group and taking advantage of the broader alliance with Delta Air Lines, Singapore Airlines and Austrian Airlines.
"Swissair and Sabena will continue to pursue these objectives," SAirGroup said. ($ = 1.434 Swiss Francs)
